stops.name: Lausanne: the Festival Vaudois, canton's centenary
stops.campa: For the hundredth anniversary of the canton of Vaud's entry into the Confederation, Jaques-Dalcroze composes the Festival vaudois, a Festspiel to match the Poème alpestre in scale: the second of the great civic pageants that will punctuate his career, always at the hinge of a Swiss canton's or city's memory of itself. Choruses drawn from villages across the canton rehearse for months; the composer conducts the mass of amateur voices as he once tried to conduct fingers that could not keep time, and finds, in the crowd instead of the classroom, the same rhythmic problem at civic scale.

stops.name: Paris, Le Bonhomme Jadis and the letter from Appia
stops.campa: His opera Le Bonhomme Jadis is staged at the Paris Opéra-Comique the same year that the Genevan scenographer Adolphe Appia, who witnessed a rhythmic-gymnastics demonstration and could not shake it from his mind, writes to him unbidden. The two Swiss reformers, one remaking the stage's light and space, the other remaking the body that moves through it, begin a correspondence that will, within four years, build a theatre together at Hellerau. Each recognizes in the other's art the missing half of his own.
stops.quote: To restore rhythm to the body, to make music vibrate within it, as to make music an integral part of one's organism, to play with this marvellous keyboard which is the muscular and nervous system, to render plastically a thought measured in space as in time, that is what I seek.
stops.quote_source: Jaques-Dalcroze, letter to Adolphe Appia, 1906 (trans. from the French; 'Rendre au corps son eurythmie...')

stops.name: Brussels, Les Jumeaux de Bergame at the Monnaie
stops.campa: The pantomime-ballet Les Jumeaux de Bergame is given at the Théâtre de la Monnaie, with Nina Faliero-Dalcroze among the singers: the composer's stage works now travelling beyond Switzerland and France into Belgium's first opera house. The reputation that carries him abroad is still, for the wider public, a composer's reputation; the rhythmic-gymnastics classroom in Geneva remains, to outsiders, a curious pedagogical sideline. Within two years the sideline will eclipse the composer, and a German garden-city will build him a theatre of his own.

stops.name: Geneva: a son, Gabriel, is born
stops.campa: A son, Gabriel, is born to Émile and Nina in Geneva: the household's own small rhythm added to the larger one the father is still building in classrooms and concert halls. Within a year the family's life will be pulled toward Saxony, as an invitation arrives from two German brothers, Wolf and Harald Dohrn, offering to build for the Geneva schoolmaster and his unruly pedagogy a garden-city temple of its own, with an unheard-of theatre attached, in a settlement called Hellerau.

stops.name: Geneva, the Conservatoire calls it 'monkeyshines'
stops.campa: The Conservatoire's administrators, scandalized by bare feet and jersey tunics in a hall meant for scales and sonatas, condemn the rhythmic-gymnastics classes as undignified monkeyshines and press for their curtailment. At the very moment the door in Geneva narrows, the letter from Wolf Dohrn arrives from the new garden-city of Hellerau outside Dresden, proposing a Bildungsanstalt built to his exact specification: studios, gardens, no administrators to scandalize. He accepts. The method that Geneva tolerated as a sideline is about to be given its own state.

stops.name: Hellerau, the Bildungsanstalt opens its doors
stops.campa: In the model garden-city of Hellerau above Dresden, reformed furniture, reformed dress, reformed bodies all manufactured on the same model estate, the Bildungsanstalt für rhythmische Gymnastik opens with 115 students crowded into still-unfinished rooms. Jaques-Dalcroze directs the whole curriculum himself: three fifty-minute morning classes in rhythmic movement, solfège and improvisation, afternoons of individual instruction and ensemble rehearsal, evenings of shared cultural life. The Conservatoire's sideline has become, almost overnight, the best-equipped school of its kind in Europe, and its founder its uncontested master.
stops.quote: The body can become a marvellous instrument of beauty and harmony when it vibrates in tune with artistic imagination and collaborates with creative thought.
stops.quote_source: Jaques-Dalcroze, 'Rhythm as a Factor in Education', in Rhythm, Music and Education (trans. Ingham, 1921)

stops.name: Hellerau: Suzanne Perrottet, the Geneva assistant
stops.campa: Among his closest collaborators at the Bildungsanstalt is Suzanne Perrottet, the young Genevan violinist who trained under him at the Conservatoire and followed him to Saxony to teach his method to Hellerau's newest pupils, Mary Wigman among them. She is exact, gifted, and, though he does not yet see it, already restless inside the very discipline she teaches so well: movement always in service of a score, never sovereign over it. Within months she will be gone, drawn up the mountain above Ascona to a Hungarian who lets his dancers move in silence.

stops.name: Hellerau: the Festspielhaus, dance as the handmaid of music
stops.campa: Under Adolphe Appia's white terraces and Alexander von Salzmann's walls of woven light, the new Festspielhaus opens its first Festspiele: two weeks of class demonstrations, the pantomime Echo et Narcisse, and, as its climax, the Descent into the Underworld from Gluck's Orphée, danced by Dalcroze's own students before some four thousand spectators and five hundred journalists drawn from every capital of Europe. Among the pupils absorbing the discipline of bar and phrase is a fierce, unfinished young woman named Marie Wiegmann, who will one day break the very obedience this stage teaches her.
stops.quote: I expect much from education in rhythm in elementary schools, provided it be given regularly, completely and sufficiently.
stops.quote_source: Jaques-Dalcroze, Dresden lecture of 1912, in Rhythm, Music and Education (trans. Ingham, 1921)

stops.name: Hellerau, the pupil who wants the body itself to be the music
stops.campa: He does not fail to notice Marie Wiegmann's discontent. She is diligent, gifted, and increasingly mutinous, drilling rhythm into her spine as required while something unnamed in her strains against the method's first article of faith: that movement exists to serve the score. The painter Emil Nolde, watching her in class, tells her plainly to go to Rudolf von Laban, who teaches without music at all. Dalcroze loses her as he lost Perrottet, to the same mountain above Ascona; he will say only, of the pupils who leave this way, that the school could teach the discipline but not always contain what it woke.

stops.name: Hellerau: the full Orfeo, and Jeanne Allemand takes her diploma
stops.campa: The second festival gives Gluck's Orfeo ed Euridice complete, Appia's terraces now fully realized in light and shadow; Prince Sergei Wolkonsky comes from the Imperial theatres, and the American teacher Susan Canfield among a wave of foreign visitors carries the method home across an ocean. Quietly, among the diploma students that same season, a young Genevan-trained pupil named Jeanne Allemand completes her rhythmics certificate and stays on to teach: the same Jeanne who will marry the painter Alexandre de Salzmann here and, within six years, carry a version of rhythmic discipline into a stranger school in Tiflis.

stops.name: Chamonix / Hellerau, the death of Wolf Dohrn
stops.campa: Wolf Dohrn, the visionary who built Hellerau for him and financed every year of it, dies in a skiing accident in the Chamonix Alps on 4 February 1914, descending from the Col de Balme in darkness, not yet thirty-six. Jaques-Dalcroze speaks the tribute at the funeral, gathered with the whole community of the garden-city he did not expect to bury its founder before its work was proven. Hellerau loses in an afternoon its driving force and its purse; the school Dohrn built will outlive him by a matter of months, not years.

stops.name: Geneva, a pageant for the Confederation's centenary
stops.campa: Commissioned three years earlier to mark the centenary of Geneva's entry into the Swiss Confederation, Jaques-Dalcroze returns from Hellerau in the spring of 1914 with his assistant Annie Beck and a cadre of senior students to rehearse La Fête de Juin: a Festspiel in five acts, libretto by Daniel Baud-Bovy and Albert Malche, built for a temporary theatre of 5,700 seats rising at the edge of the Perle du Lac park. He does not yet know he is leaving Hellerau for good; he believes, like everyone that spring, that he will simply go back after the summer.
